section.title: The Seven and the Martyrdom of Stephen
section.sectionRationale: A practical crisis over the neglected Grecian widows leads the Twelve to appoint seven Spirit-filled men, freeing the apostles for prayer and the word, and the church surges. One of the seven, Stephen, full of grace and power, provokes fierce opposition, is seized on false charges of speaking against the temple and the law, and is dragged before the Sanhedrin. His long speech retells Israel's story to show that God has always worked outside the holy places and that Israel has always resisted His messengers, climaxing in the charge that they have now betrayed and murdered the Righteous One. Enraged, they stone him, and Stephen dies as his Lord did, seeing the Son of Man and praying for his killers, while a young man named Saul looks on.
section.thesis: The God of glory has never been confined to land or temple but has moved with His people from Abraham to the present, and just as Israel rejected Joseph and Moses and the prophets, so it has now rejected and murdered the Righteous One; yet the risen Christ stands at God's right hand to receive His faithful witness, and Stephen's Christlike death, forgiving his enemies, becomes a seed of the mission that Saul will one day carry to the nations.
section.frameNote: Nine movements: the choosing of the seven; the arrest of Stephen on false charges; his speech tracing God with Abraham, with Joseph, with Moses born and rejected, with Moses the redeemer amid Israel's rebellion, and through tabernacle to temple; his climactic indictment; and his martyrdom, forgiving his killers as Saul watches.

units.label: The choosing of the Seven
units.note: the widows are cared for and the word of God spreads

verses.text: In those days when the disciples were increasing in number, the Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.
So the Twelve summoned all the disciples and said, “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.
Therefore, brothers, select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will assign this responsibility to them
and will devote ourselves to prayer and to the {{diakonia|ministry}} of the word.”

This proposal pleased the whole group. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, as well as Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism.
They presented these seven to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
So the word of God continued to spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem grew rapidly, and a great number of priests became obedient to the faith.

units.label: The arrest of Stephen
units.note: false witnesses charge him against the temple and the law

verses.text: Now Stephen, who was full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people.
But resistance arose from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, including Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and men from the provinces of Cilicia and Asia. They disputed with Stephen,
but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke.
Then they prompted some men to say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God.”
So they stirred up the people, elders, and scribes and confronted Stephen. They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin,
where they presented false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law.
For we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”
All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

units.label: The God of glory and the call of Abraham
units.note: God appears and promises before there is any land or temple

verses.text: Then the high priest asked Stephen, “Are these charges true?”
And Stephen declared: “Brothers and fathers, listen to me! The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran,
and told him, ‘Leave your country and your kindred and go to the land I will show you.’
So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God brought him out of that place and into this land where you are now living.
He gave him no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground. But God promised to give possession of the land to Abraham and his descendants, even though he did not yet have a child.
God told him that his descendants would be foreigners in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years.
‘But I will punish the nation that enslaves them,’ God said, ‘and afterward they will come forth and worship Me in this place.’

Then God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

units.label: Joseph, rejected by his brothers yet used to save
units.note: God is with the rejected one in a foreign land

verses.text: Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him
and rescued him from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household.
Then famine and great suffering swept across Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food.
When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers on their first visit.
On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh.
Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five in all.
So Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our fathers died.
Their bones were carried back to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a price he paid in silver.

units.label: Moses born and rejected by his own
units.note: the appointed deliverer is pushed aside by the people he came to help

verses.text: As the time drew near for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham, our people in Egypt increased greatly in number.
Then another king, who knew nothing of Joseph, arose over Egypt.
He exploited our people and oppressed our fathers, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would die.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in the sight of God. For three months he was nurtured in his father’s house.
When he was set outside, Pharaoh’s daughter took him and brought him up as her own son.
So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action.
When Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his brothers, the children of Israel.
And when he saw one of them being mistreated, Moses went to his defense and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian who was oppressing him.
He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not.
The next day he came upon two Israelites who were fighting, and he tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you mistreating each other?’
But the man who was abusing his neighbor pushed Moses aside and said, ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons.

units.label: Moses the redeemer, and Israel's rebellion
units.note: the rejected one is sent as ruler and redeemer, yet Israel turns to idols

verses.text: After forty years had passed, an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a burning bush in the desert near Mount Sinai.
When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight. As he approached to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came to him:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’ Moses trembled with fear and did not dare to look.
Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have indeed seen the oppression of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt.’
This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
He led them out and performed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and for forty years in the wilderness.
This is the same Moses who told the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’
He was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. And he received living words to pass on to us.
But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.
They said to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us! As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’
At that time they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their hands.

But God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You have taken along the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

units.label: From tabernacle to temple: the Most High is not confined
units.note: the God of heaven and earth does not dwell in houses made by hands

verses.text: Our fathers had the tabernacle of the Testimony with them in the wilderness. It was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen.
And our fathers who received it brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations God drove out before them. It remained until the time of David,
who found favor in the sight of God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.
But it was Solomon who built the house for Him.
However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says:
‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be?
Has not My hand made all these things?’

units.label: The indictment: you always resist the Holy Spirit
units.note: as your fathers rejected the messengers, you have betrayed the Righteous One

verses.text: You {{stiffNecked|stiff-necked}} people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.
Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the {{dikaios|Righteous One}}. And now you are His betrayers and murderers,
you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it.”

units.label: The martyrdom of Stephen
units.note: he sees the Son of Man, forgives his killers, and falls asleep as Saul looks on

verses.text: On hearing this, the members of the Sanhedrin were enraged, and they gnashed their teeth at him.
But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
“Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the {{sonOfMan|Son of Man}} standing at the right hand of God.”
At this they covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him.
They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he {{koimao|fell asleep}}.

diakonia.gloss: Service, ministry, the practical work of meeting needs; the related verb lies behind waiting on tables. Luke sets the two side by side, the daily service of food and the ministry of the word, and treats both as diakonia, honorable service in the church. The seven are appointed so that neither the widows nor the word is neglected, and from this humble table service Stephen and Philip rise to powerful gospel work.

stiffNecked.gloss: Stiff-necked, obstinate, hard of neck like an ox that will not bend to the yoke. It is the very word God used of Israel at Sinai after the golden calf. Stephen turns their own Scriptures on his judges: the people who accuse him of dishonoring Moses are the true heirs of the wilderness generation, resisting the Spirit and refusing to bow to God's word and His Messiah.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, just, the Righteous One. Used as a title, it names Jesus as the sinless, wholly just servant whose coming the prophets foretold. Stephen's charge is devastating: the prophets who announced the Righteous One were persecuted, and now the council has betrayed and murdered the Righteous One Himself, adding the greatest sin to the pattern of their fathers.

sonOfMan.gloss: Son of Man, the title Jesus most often used of Himself, drawn from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. This is the only time in Acts that the title is spoken by someone other than Jesus. Stephen sees the exalted Son of Man standing to receive him, confirming that the crucified Jesus is the enthroned Lord of Daniel's vision.

koimao.gloss: To fall asleep, a tender word the New Testament uses for the death of believers. Stephen is stoned in fury, yet Luke says he fell asleep, for death has been disarmed by the risen Christ into whose hands he commits his spirit. The violent martyrdom is described with the gentleness of rest, because the one who receives him is the Lord of life.

basic.context: The growing church hits a practical problem: the Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles will not abandon prayer and the word, so seven Spirit-filled men are chosen to oversee the service, and the church keeps growing. One of them, Stephen, does great signs and stirs fierce opposition. False witnesses accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law, and he is dragged before the Sanhedrin. His long reply retells Israel's history, showing that God worked long before there was any temple and that Israel always rejected His chosen messengers. When he charges them with murdering the Righteous One and sees the Son of Man in heaven, they stone him, and he dies forgiving them, watched by a young man named Saul.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the speech as Stephen's answer to two charges, that he attacked the temple and the law. He does not deny God's gifts of law and temple; he shows they were never meant to box God in, and that the real problem is a people who resist the Spirit. The history is not a detour; every stage, Joseph, Moses, the prophets, builds one point: God's people keep rejecting the ones God sends, and now they have done it to Jesus. The martyrdom is deliberately told to echo Jesus' own death.
basic.originalLanguages: A few words carry the section. The seven are set over the diakonia, the service, so the apostles can give themselves to the ministry of the word. Stephen calls his judges stiff-necked, sklerotrachelos, the exact term God used of Israel after the golden calf. He names Jesus the dikaios, the Righteous One, whom they betrayed and murdered. And he sees the Son of Man, the huios tou anthropou of Daniel 7, standing in heaven, before he falls asleep, koimao, the gentle word for a believer's death.
basic.typology: Joseph, rejected by his brothers yet raised to save them, and Moses, pushed aside by his own people yet sent as their ruler and redeemer, both foreshadow Jesus, rejected by Israel yet exalted to save. The prophet like Moses whom God promised is Christ. The tabernacle and temple point beyond themselves to the God who fills heaven and earth and finally to Christ, in whom God dwells with His people.
basic.christ: Jesus is the pattern's climax: the rejected Joseph, the rejected Moses, the prophet like Moses, and above all the Righteous One whom the prophets foretold and this generation murdered. At the end He appears as the Son of Man standing at God's right hand to welcome His witness. Stephen dies as Jesus did, entrusting his spirit to the Lord and praying forgiveness for his killers, so that his death is stamped with the death of Christ.
basic.god: God is the God of glory who appears to Abraham in pagan Mesopotamia, who is with Joseph in Egypt, who speaks to Moses in a desert bush, and who fills heaven and earth so that no house can contain Him. He is faithful to His promises across centuries, patient with a rebellious people, and just in His judgment. He receives His faithful servant into glory even as men rage.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12 records the call of Abraham that opens the speech. Deuteronomy 18:15 promises the prophet like Moses, fulfilled in Jesus. Isaiah 66:1-2 declares that no house can contain the Most High. Luke 23:34 and 23:46 give Jesus' words that Stephen echoes in his dying prayers.
basic.oneStory: The ascended Christ pours out His Spirit, and the gospel, resisted in Jerusalem, is about to break its bounds. Stephen shows that God was never trapped in the temple and that His people have always rejected His messengers, right up to the Righteous One. His Christlike death is not the end but a seed: scattered by the persecution that follows, the church will carry the word into Judea, Samaria, and beyond, and the very Saul who guards the coats will become the apostle to the nations.

context.literary:
Acts 6:1 to 7:60 is the hinge of the book. Everything before it happens in and around Jerusalem; everything after it moves outward. Luke shows the turn by letting two trials overlap. Stephen stands before the same Sanhedrin that questioned Peter and John in Acts 4 and 5, and the charge brought against him, that he threatens the temple, is the one that was brought against Jesus, Mark 14:57-58. The reader is meant to feel the trial of the Master sliding over the trial of the servant.

The unit is a diptych. In 6:1-7 a problem inside the church is solved wisely and the word grows. In 6:8 to 7:60 a problem outside the church is met with a long speech, and the speech is answered with stones. Luke brackets the whole with a refrain: 'the word of God continued to spread,' 6:7, and then 'those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went,' 8:4. The death of Stephen sits inside the growth of the word, not against it.

The speech has a clear architecture. Verses 2 to 16 cover Abraham and the patriarchs, verses 17 to 43 Moses, verses 44 to 50 the tabernacle and the temple, and verses 51 to 53 turn from story to accusation. It belongs with Israel's other recitals of her own history, Psalm 78, Psalm 106, Nehemiah 9 and Joshua 24, and it resembles the sorrowful ones. Its hinge is the repeated 'this Moses' of verses 35, 37 and 40. The man they pushed aside is the man God sent; the man they turned back to Egypt in their hearts to forget is the man who promised another prophet like himself. Stephen does not answer the charge by argument. He answers by retelling, and only at the end does he apply.

Two small repetitions frame the scene. In 6:15 the council 'looked intently' at Stephen and saw a face like an angel's; in 7:55 Stephen 'looked intently into heaven' and saw the glory of God. The council fixes its gaze on him; he fixes his on the One they cannot see.
context.historical:
Jerusalem in these years held Jews from across the Mediterranean world. The two groups of 6:1 were divided mainly by language and background. The Hebraic Jews spoke Aramaic and Hebrew, while the Grecian Jews, in Greek Hellenistai, spoke Greek and many had settled in the city from the diaspora. A widow with no family nearby had no one to carry her, which is why a daily distribution mattered so much. Care for the widow is a mark of God's people in the Law, Deuteronomy 14:29 and 24:19-21. All seven men chosen bear Greek names, which suggests the church placed the repair in the hands of the group that had been hurt. Nicolas is named as a proselyte from Antioch, and Antioch is where the scattered believers will first speak to Greeks, Acts 11:19-20.

The Synagogue of the Freedmen drew men from North Africa, Egypt, Cilicia and Asia, 6:9. Jerusalem had many synagogues, each serving a language community, and a Greek speaker like Stephen would naturally argue in them. Cilicia was Saul's province, Acts 21:39, which may help explain why Saul is on the scene.

The charge touched what the city lived by. The temple was the centre of worship, income and national pride, and the priestly leaders held their power under Roman oversight. Speaking against it had always been dangerous: Jeremiah was seized and told 'You must surely die' for warning that the house would fall like Shiloh, Jeremiah 26:8-9. Stoning was the biblical penalty for blasphemy, Leviticus 24:14-16, and the witnesses threw first, Deuteronomy 17:7. The garments laid at Saul's feet show the witnesses stripping off their outer cloaks for that duty.

Stephen's history follows the Greek Old Testament in places. The seventy-five of 7:14 matches the Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, where the Hebrew text reads seventy. A Greek-speaking audience would have known exactly that wording.
context.canonical:
Stephen takes his place in a long line of Scripture's own judgments on Israel. Nehemiah 9:26 confesses that the fathers killed the prophets who warned them. Jesus said the same thing in sharper terms, charging His generation with all the righteous blood shed 'from the blood of righteous Abel' onward, Matthew 23:35, and telling the parable of the tenants who killed the owner's son, Luke 20:9-16. Stephen's last question, 'Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute?', stands inside that tradition.

The temple thread is just as old. Solomon himself said at the dedication that even the highest heaven cannot contain God, much less the house he had built, 1 Kings 8:27, and Nathan's word to David had already asked who had requested a house, 2 Samuel 7:5-7. Isaiah 66:1-2 puts the matter in God's own voice, and Jeremiah 7 turns it against those who chanted that this was the temple of the LORD while living in rebellion. In the New Testament the thread runs on through Jesus' word about the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, the end of the holy mountain as the only place of worship, John 4:21-24, the church as God's dwelling, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:19-22, and the city where John sees no temple at all, Revelation 21:22.

The Righteous One is a title with deep roots, from Isaiah 53:11, 'My righteous Servant,' to Peter's sermon, Acts 3:14, and Ananias's word to Saul, Acts 22:14. The death of Stephen opens the persecution that sends the church out, Acts 8:1 and 11:19, and Paul never forgets it, Acts 22:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke writes to show how the church came to leave Jerusalem. The reader has watched the word grow in the temple courts; here the leaders finally set themselves against it, and the speech explains why. He wants Theophilus and every later reader to see that the gospel is not a break with Israel's story but its fulfilment, and that those who reject it are repeating a very old habit rather than defending an old faith.

He is also careful to protect Stephen's reputation. The charges are called false, 6:13, and the speech is given in full so that readers can judge for themselves what he actually said. Stephen is not a radical against Moses; he is the one who quotes Moses, 7:37, and who says the law was received by angels, 7:53.

Finally Luke wants the reader to see how a Christian dies. The unit's last lines are not the stones but the words, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'do not hold this sin against them,' set in the mouth of the first believer to follow his Lord all the way to death. The introduction of Saul at the foot of the scene is deliberate: the one who minds the coats is the one who will carry this name further than any other.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The speech is a model of Spirit-given witness, but it is not a template for how to talk to opponents. Stephen's hard words in 7:51-53 describe what he was given to say on one occasion to one council that had already killed the Master; they do not license harshness in ordinary conversation. Elsewhere Luke shows Paul reasoning with unbelievers from the Scriptures, Acts 17:2-3, and Peter tells believers to answer with gentleness and respect, 1 Peter 3:15.

The appointment of the seven is likewise a record. Luke does not say that every church must create seven deacons, nor even that these men were called deacons; the verb for serving, diakoneo, appears of the tables, 6:2, while the noun is used for both the tables and the word, 6:1 and 6:4. What carries forward is the principle: a real need gets a real, wise, Spirit-led answer, and the teaching of the word is not allowed to be crowded out.

Stephen's death is described, not commanded. Believers are not told to seek martyrdom. They are shown how to face it, with the Lord in view and forgiveness on the lips.

debates.question: Does Stephen's speech condemn the temple itself, or only its idolatrous misuse?

views.label: It condemns trusting in the temple, not the temple as God's gift
views.case: Stephen affirms that God directed the tabernacle and that Solomon built the house, 7:44-47, yet quotes Isaiah 66:1-2 that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Solomon said much the same at the dedication, 1 Kings 8:27. The target is the presumption that God can be contained or that possessing the building secures His favour.

views.label: It announces that the temple's role is passing in God's plan
views.case: By stressing that God met Abraham, Joseph and Moses far from Jerusalem, and by using for the temple the word that the Greek Old Testament uses for idols, Stephen signals that the building's era is giving way now that Christ has come. The charge in 6:14 was a distortion of something true, since Jesus spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21.

debates.bearing: Both agree Stephen honours the temple as God's gift while denying it can bind Him. They differ on how final his point is, and the answer shapes how one reads Hebrews and the church as the new dwelling.

debates.question: Why does Stephen see Jesus standing rather than seated?

views.label: Standing to receive and welcome His witness
views.case: Psalm 110:1 and Luke 22:69 picture the Son of Man seated at God's right hand. Standing is a posture of readiness, so many read the verse as the ascended Lord rising to meet His first martyr, the One who promised to confess before the angels those who confess Him, Luke 12:8.

views.label: Standing as witness, advocate or judge
views.case: In the Old Testament a heavenly court is pictured with the judge on a throne and others standing to testify or to act. On this reading Jesus stands as Stephen's advocate, or as the Son of Man about to judge the council that is judging His servant, with 'seated' language describing His enthronement and 'standing' describing a moment of action.

debates.bearing: The verse does not say why, so neither reading should be pressed hard. Either way the point is plain: the One they condemned is alive, is at God's right hand, and is attentive to His servant.

debates.question: How should we handle the differences between Stephen's retelling and the Old Testament?

views.label: Stephen follows the Greek text and Jewish tradition, and Luke reports his words faithfully
views.case: The seventy-five in 7:14 matches the Septuagint, not the Hebrew. Abraham's call in Mesopotamia, 7:2, agrees with Genesis 15:7 and Nehemiah 9:7. Luke records what Stephen said, much as Scripture records what others said, without endorsing every detail.

views.label: The details harmonise on a careful reading
views.case: Abraham purchased a field and tomb at Machpelah, Genesis 23, while Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, Genesis 33:19, where Joseph's bones were laid, Joshua 24:32. Verse 16 may compress two purchases and two burials into one summary. The 'beyond Babylon' of 7:43 for Amos's 'beyond Damascus,' Amos 5:27, would then be a deliberate update, since Babylon was where the exile actually ended.

debates.bearing: Neither reading touches the main argument, which does not rest on a number or a burial site. Readers who hold to the full truthfulness of Scripture can take either path, and should avoid forcing a harmony where the text does not give one.

study.originalLanguages:
The complaint of 6:1 names two groups, the Hellenistai and the Hebraioi, a division of language and culture within one faith. Luke's solution uses a single root three ways. The widows were overlooked in the daily diakonia, the distribution, 6:1. The apostles refuse to diakonein trapezais, to serve tables, 6:2, and will give themselves to prayer and the diakonia of the word, 6:4. Luke does not rank one service above the other as a lesser or greater kind. He only says that each needs its own people, and he gives the table to men full of the Spirit and wisdom.

Twice in the unit the verb atenizo, to look intently, is used: of the council looking at Stephen, 6:15, and of Stephen looking into heaven, 7:55. It is a staring that cannot be turned aside, and Luke uses it of the disciples looking after the ascending Christ in Acts 1:10. In this scene it marks the contrast between those who look at a face and the man who looks at the Lord.

In 7:38 Moses received logia zonta, living words. The adjective is the point. The law was not a dead document but a living utterance from the God who speaks, and the same verse calls Israel's gathering in the wilderness the ekklesia, the assembly or church. Stephen's own people are the church of the wilderness, and the quarrel is about whether they will go on as the assembly of the living God.

The word for the temple in 7:48, cheiropoietos, made by hands, is the word for manufactured things. The Septuagint uses it of idols, and in 7:41 Luke has already told us that the calf was 'the works of their hands.' Stephen does not call the temple an idol, but the vocabulary puts a shadow beside it, and it matches the false witness in Mark 14:58 of a temple 'made' by hands.

In 7:52 the leaders are prodotai kai phoneis, betrayers and murderers. The pairing recalls Judas's betrayal and Pilate's trial and puts the council in the same company. The word for the first, prodotes, appears of Judas in Luke 6:16.

Finally, in 7:59 Stephen is epikaloumenos, calling upon the Lord Jesus, the verb of Joel 2:32 and Acts 2:21, and the very mark of believers in Acts 9:14. His last prayer, mē stēsēs autois tautēn tēn hamartian, is literally 'do not make this sin stand against them,' as an entry set to their account. It echoes the Lord's forgiving words in Luke 23:34. Even Stephen's name, Stephanos, means a crown or wreath, and the crown of martyrdom is the first one laid on a believer in Acts.

typology.type: Joseph, sold by his brothers and raised to rule, Acts 7:9-14
typology.fulfillment: Stephen tells Joseph's story with two phrases that matter, 'the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph' and 'God was with him,' 7:9. The pattern is rejection by his own, exaltation through suffering, and a second visit on which he is recognised and the family restored, 7:13. In Jesus the pattern is complete: sold for silver, Matthew 26:15, delivered by the jealousy of the leaders, Mark 15:10, and now exalted at God's right hand, Acts 2:33, so that the brothers who rejected Him may be saved by Him. The type falls short in that Joseph's brothers were forgiven in a famine and a family; those who deny Jesus must be forgiven at a cross and by faith.

typology.type: Moses, rejected as ruler and sent as redeemer, Acts 7:35
typology.fulfillment: The people said, 'Who made you ruler and judge?' and God sent that same man as ruler and redeemer, 7:35. Stephen insists that the redeemer was disowned before he redeemed. In Jesus the pattern repeats and deepens: He was rejected at Pilate's bar, 'we have no king but Caesar,' John 19:15, and God has made Him 'both Lord and Christ,' Acts 2:36. Moses led his people out through the sea; Christ leads people out of death, Hebrews 2:14-15. The type falls short because Moses, the greatest of servants, was only a servant in the house, while Christ is the Son over it, Hebrews 3:5-6.

typology.type: The tabernacle built to a pattern, Acts 7:44
typology.fulfillment: The tent of the Testimony was built, Stephen says, 'according to the pattern he had seen,' echoing Exodus 25:40. The pattern was a copy and shadow of what is in heaven, Hebrews 8:5. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled: God pitched His tent among us, John 1:14, the body of Jesus is the true temple, John 2:19-21, and His people are being built into a dwelling for God by the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short because every earthly sanctuary needed repeated sacrifices and could not remove sin, while Christ entered once for all, Hebrews 9:11-12.

typology.type: Joshua, who brought the fathers into the land, Acts 7:45
typology.fulfillment: In 7:45 the Greek names Joshua with the same name as Jesus, Iesous, and it is Joshua who led the fathers into possession of the land God promised. Hebrews 4:8 notes that Joshua did not give the people final rest, which implies a greater Joshua. Jesus leads His people to the rest that Joshua's land only pointed to, Hebrews 4:9-11, a land that is not one stretch of ground but the new creation. The type falls short at every point where Joshua's rest is partial and temporary, with enemies still in the land and a temple to be built, while Christ's rest is complete.

study.christ:
Stephen's speech is Christ-centred even though Jesus is not named until the very end. The whole history is told so that it ends at a person, and the person is introduced in two phrases. The first is 'the Righteous One,' 7:52, who stands behind Isaiah's 'righteous Servant,' Isaiah 53:11, and whom Ananias will later say Saul is to see, Acts 22:14. The second is the Son of Man at God's right hand, 7:56.

The prophet like Moses is the speech's quiet centre. In 7:37 Stephen quotes Deuteronomy 18:15 right in the middle of his Moses section: 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.' Peter has already applied it to Jesus, Acts 3:22-23, and Stephen's point is that the people who turned on the first Moses are about to turn on the second. The words Moses received were 'living words,' and the One who comes after him is called the Word, John 1:1, whose words are spirit and life, John 6:63.

The vision at the end completes the picture. The Son of Man of Daniel 7:13-14, who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days, is now seen, and Jesus' own word at His trial, 'from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God,' Luke 22:69, is shown to be true. The council hears Stephen claim to see Him there and covers its ears. It is the second time that day it has refused the witness of the Son.

Stephen's death is also Christlike in many details: a charge about the temple, false witnesses, a council, a prayer entrusting his spirit, Luke 23:46, and a prayer of forgiveness, Luke 23:34. The echoes are not accidents of style. They are the way Luke says that the Lord who stands in heaven is also the Lord who is living in His servant on earth. The union that Saul will meet on the Damascus road, 'why do you persecute Me?', Acts 9:4, is already at work here.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Not every detail of the speech is a hidden picture of Jesus. Stephen himself draws out the links that matter: the rejected deliverer, the prophet like Moses, the house not made with hands, and the Righteous One betrayed. The rest of the history is there to show Israel's pattern, and Christ is its end.
study.god:
The speech opens with a name for God, 'the God of glory,' 7:2, and the whole address argues from it. The glory that appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before there was a land, a law or a temple, is not tied to any of them. Psalm 29:3 uses the title of the God who thunders over the waters, and Stephen uses it for the God who walks out into pagan territory to call a man.

God is shown as the one who takes the initiative at every point of the history. He appears to Abraham, 7:2; he is with Joseph in Egypt, 7:9; He sees and hears the oppression and comes down to deliver, 7:34. The verbs of the speech belong to God, and the verbs of Israel are the opposite: they were jealous, refused, rejected, turned back, made a calf, resisted. The doctrine of grace is told as a history before it is told as a doctrine.

God is also the God who is not contained. 'The Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands,' 7:48. He gave the pattern for the tent and allowed Solomon to build, yet He is the one whose hand made all things, 7:50. This is no denial of His nearness, since He was with Abraham, Joseph and Moses where there was no building. It is an insistence that His presence comes by His own choice and not by human arrangement.

He is just. The people's refusal brought judgment: He 'turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven,' 7:42, an echo of Romans 1:24. Yet He is patient: Stephen can tell the whole history of rebellion because God continued to send deliverers, from Joseph to Moses to the prophets to the Righteous One.

He receives His witnesses. The glory that Stephen sees and the Jesus at God's right hand show the Father open to the one who dies. For worship, the unit teaches that God is found where He chooses to be found, in the word, in the Son, and by the Spirit, and that nobody who clings to a place or a tradition while resisting the Spirit has really found Him.

crossReferences.note: Stephen says God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before Haran. Genesis 15:7 says the LORD brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans, confirming that the call began there. The point of the opening is that God's glory met Abraham in a pagan land with no temple and no law.

God calls the people 'a stiff-necked people' at the golden calf. Stephen's 'stiff-necked' in 7:51 deliberately takes the charge from the foundation story, so that his hearers are named with the title God gave their fathers when they made the calf.

The promise of a prophet like Moses stands at the centre of Stephen's account of Moses, 7:37. Peter has already applied it to Jesus in Acts 3:22-23. Stephen's argument is that the people who rejected the first deliverer are about to reject the greater one.

Solomon, who built the house, says at its dedication that even the highest heaven cannot contain God, much less this temple. Stephen's point in 7:47-50 is therefore not new; it is the temple builder's own confession, which later generations had forgotten.

Quoted almost in full in 7:49-50. God asks what house they could build for Him and then says whom He esteems: the humble and contrite who tremble at His word. The unit's contrast is between that trembling and the council's rage.

Jeremiah was seized and called worthy of death for speaking against the temple and the city. Stephen is charged with the same offence for the same reason, and the passage shows how often God's messengers were treated as enemies of the house they were trying to save.

Jesus promised His witnesses speech and wisdom that no adversary could resist or contradict. Acts 6:10 says Stephen's opponents 'could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke.' The promise is fulfilled in him.

Jesus prays forgiveness for those who crucify Him. Stephen's 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them,' 7:60, is the same prayer, now addressed to Jesus as Lord. The pupil's death is shaped by the Master's.

Jesus commits His spirit into the Father's hands. Stephen says, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,' 7:59. The words are addressed to Jesus Himself, a sign that for Luke the Son shares in the Father's care of the dying.

Paul remembers the day Stephen died as 'the blood of Your witness Stephen,' and himself standing there giving approval and minding the garments of the killers. The word witness is the root of martyr, and it shows how long this scene lived in the mind of the man who watched.

The writer quotes Exodus 25:40, the pattern Moses saw on the mountain, to say that the tabernacle was a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. It is the same pattern Stephen mentions in 7:44, now read in the light of Christ.

study.oneStory:
The question Stephen answers is the oldest in the book: where does God meet His people, and why do they keep turning from Him? Genesis opens with God walking in a garden, and loses that place at the fall. From then on, the story of Scripture is the search for the place where God and man can meet again. Abraham receives a promise and no ground. Israel receives a tent in the wilderness, then a temple in the city. Each of them is a gift, and each becomes something people hide behind. Stephen's speech reads the whole story as a record of God coming out to meet people in every place, wherever there was no building, and of people shutting out the One who came.

The rejection is also an old pattern. Abel was killed by his brother in the opening chapters, Cain's rage is the first of the line that Jesus lists, and the prophets were pursued to the end. The Righteous One is the last in the series and the first of a new kind, because His blood does not call for vengeance but speaks a better word, Hebrews 12:24.

After Stephen the story turns on a single sentence in Acts 8:1: the church is scattered, and the word goes with them. The persecution that follows his death carries the gospel to Samaria, to Antioch and, through the young man at the coats, to the Gentile world. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed, which Stephen has just recalled, is on its way to its fulfilment.

The end of the story is the temple question answered. John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, and the Son of Man whom Stephen saw standing is the one at the centre of that city. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia will in the end dwell with His people in a place that no one has to build.

quiz.q: Why did the apostles have the church choose seven men?

options.text: So the Grecian widows would be cared for while the apostles kept devoting themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 give both the need and the apostles' priority.

options.text: Because the Grecian widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution.
options.note: True, this was the trigger, but the fuller reason includes guarding the ministry of the word.

options.text: Because the apostles no longer wished to serve anyone at tables.
options.note: It was not distaste for service but a matter of calling and priority; both tasks are honored as ministry.

options.text: Because the church needed officials to manage its money and property.
options.note: The concern was caring for widows and preserving the word, not general administration.

quiz.q: What was the thrust of the false charges against Stephen?

options.text: That he never stopped speaking against the temple and the law, saying Jesus would destroy the place and change Moses' customs.
options.note: Verses 13 to 14 give the accusation about the holy place and the law.

options.text: That he had spoken blasphemy against Moses and against God.
options.note: True, from verse 11, but the formal charges before the council centered on the temple and the law.

options.text: That he had led a violent revolt against Rome.
options.note: The charges were religious, about the temple and the law, not political rebellion.

options.text: That he had stolen from the common fund of the church.
options.note: No such charge appears; the accusations concerned the temple and the law.

quiz.q: What is the main point Stephen's retelling of Israel's history makes?

options.text: God has always worked beyond the holy places, and Israel has always resisted the messengers He sends, now even the Righteous One.
options.note: The speech traces God with Abraham, Joseph, and Moses and climaxes in the charge of resisting the Spirit and murdering Jesus.

options.text: God cannot be contained in a temple made by human hands.
options.note: A key strand, from verses 48 to 50, but part of the larger point about resisting God's messengers.

options.text: The law and the temple were always mistakes that God never wanted.
options.note: Stephen affirms God gave the tabernacle pattern and living words; the fault is idolizing them and resisting the Spirit, not the gifts themselves.

options.text: Israel's history proves that God had abandoned His promises to Abraham.
options.note: The opposite; Stephen shows God faithfully keeping His promises across the centuries.

quiz.q: What did Stephen see as he was about to be killed?

options.text: The glory of God and the Son of Man, Jesus, standing at the right hand of God.
options.note: Verses 55 to 56 record his vision of the exalted Christ.

options.text: Heaven opened above the Sanhedrin.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the heart of the vision was Jesus, the Son of Man, standing at God's right hand.

options.text: An angel coming to carry him bodily out of the city.
options.note: No such rescue is described; he saw the exalted Jesus and was then stoned.

options.text: A vision of the temple restored in splendor.
options.note: He saw the risen Christ in heaven, not a restored temple.

quiz.q: How does Stephen's death mirror the death of Jesus?

options.text: He entrusted his spirit to the Lord and prayed forgiveness for his killers, as Jesus did.
options.note: Verses 59 to 60 echo Jesus' words in Luke 23:46 and 23:34.

options.text: He cried out in a loud voice as he died.
options.note: True, but the deeper likeness is committing his spirit to the Lord and forgiving his enemies.

options.text: He was crucified outside the city like Jesus.
options.note: He was stoned, not crucified, though he did suffer outside the city; the real parallel is his words and spirit.

options.text: He called down judgment on those who stoned him.
options.note: He did the opposite, praying that the sin not be held against them.

quiz.q: Who is introduced at Stephen's stoning, and how?

options.text: Saul, at whose feet the witnesses laid their garments, consenting to the killing.
options.note: Verse 58 introduces Saul guarding the coats, setting up his later story.

options.text: A young man named Saul who was present at the scene.
options.note: True but understated; the witnesses laid their cloaks at his feet, marking his approval of the deed.

options.text: Gamaliel, who tried to stop the stoning.
options.note: Gamaliel appears earlier in Acts 5; the one introduced here is Saul, and he does not intervene.

options.text: Barnabas, who came to defend Stephen.
options.note: Barnabas is not present here; the figure introduced is Saul, who consents to the stoning.

questions: The church solved the widows' crisis by honoring both practical service and the ministry of the word. Where might God be calling you to serve quietly at the tables, and how do you value such service in your own church?

Stephen showed that God met Abraham, Joseph, and Moses far from any holy place. Are you tempted to confine God to certain buildings, rituals, or seasons, and how does His freedom reshape your worship?
Israel repeatedly rejected the messengers God sent. Where do you sense yourself resisting what God is saying through His word or His people, and what would it mean to soften a stiff neck?
Stephen saw the Son of Man standing to receive him in the moment of his suffering. How does the reality of the reigning, welcoming Christ steady you when you face hostility or fear?
Stephen died praying that his killers' sin would not be held against them. Who is hardest for you to forgive, and what would it look like to entrust them, and yourself, to the Lord?
The young man Saul, who approved this death, became the great apostle to the nations. Whom have you written off as beyond God's reach, and how does Saul's story enlarge your hope and your prayers?

translationNotes.note: Grecian Jews and Hebraic Jews render the Hellenists and the Hebrews; the distinction is largely linguistic and cultural, Greek-speaking against Aramaic-speaking believers.
Seventy-five in all follows the Greek Old Testament count for Jacob's household; the Hebrew of Genesis 46 reads seventy. Stephen quotes the Septuagint familiar to his hearers.
The verse compresses two burial traditions, at Shechem and near Hebron; Stephen telescopes the patriarchal accounts, a common summarizing style, without contradicting the fuller record in Genesis.
The quotation of Amos 5:25-27 follows the Greek Old Testament, which reads Rephan where the Hebrew has Kaiwan, and beyond Babylon where Amos says beyond Damascus, updating the place of exile.
The Righteous One translates ho dikaios, a title for the sinless Messiah; the thought flows on into verse 53, you who received the law.
